newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN council must expand beyond Germany, Japan:group.
newsitem.headline: UN council must expand beyond Germany, Japan:group.

text.p: The outgoing president of the U.N. General Assembly said on Monday the Security Council should be expanded beyond the addition of Germany and Japan as permanent members to include other nations too.

"The proposal that the enlargement should consist only in the entry into permanent membership of Germany and Japan alone has been dropped," Diogo Freitas do Amaral of Portugal said, citing the prevailing opinion of a U.N. working group.
He was answering reporters questions prior to Tuesday's opening of a new session of the 185-member Assembly at which Malaysian U.N. envoy Ismail Razali is to be elected president.

A U.N. working group set up nearly three years ago has been wrestling with the question of enlarging the 15-member Security Council and ensuring equitable representation on the organ responsible for international peace and security. While agreement was reached early on the need for expansion, no consensus exists on how that should be achieved.

Freitas do Amaral said a third proposal for enlargement had emerged, in addition to one for adding two countries from the developed Northern hemisphere and three from the developing South, and an Italian proposal for quasi-permanent members chosen from among countries that made significant financial and troop contributions to the United Nations.
He said the third proposal was for the establishment of five new permanent council seats, to be filled by rotation among the members of each of the U.N.'s five regional groups.

"There is also wide agreement in the working group that, should there be no enlargement in permanent membership, one should nevertheless go ahead with some degree of enlargement in non-permanent membership," he added.
There could be no reform of the council against the wishes of its current five permanent veto-bearing members -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France -- he said.

Regarding the financial plight of the United Nations, owed some $2.9 billion in peacekeeping and regular budget dues for this and previous years, Freitas do Amaral said he hoped a start would be made in January towards solving the problem.

"I very much hope it will be because, if it won't, I can see big trouble coming over the United Nations," he said. "Which means, to be very frank and candid, that we need to see ... the United States begin paying their arrears. I cannot be more frank and clear than that."
According to U.N. figures, the United States currently owes some $1.6 billion, or more than half the total arrears.
